module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 770

*References:*
 - [erdosproblems.com/770](https://www.erdosproblems.com/770)
 - [Er49d] Erdös, P. "On the strong law of large numbers." Transactions of the American Mathematical
    Society 67.1 (1949): 51-56.
 - [Ma66] Matsuyama, Noboru. "On the strong law of large numbers." Tohoku Mathematical Journal,
    Second Series 18.3 (1966): 259-269.
-/

@[expose] public section

open Set ENat Filter

namespace Erdos770


/-- Let $h n$ be the minimal number such that $2 ^ n - 1, \dots, h(n) ^ n - 1$
are collectively coprime. -/
noncomputable def h (n : ℕ) : ℕ∞ := sInf {m | 2 < m ∧
  ((Finset.Icc 2 m.toNat).image fun i => (i ^ n - 1)).gcd id = 1}

/-- `n + 1` is prime iff `h n = n + 1`. This is described as 'easy to see' in [Er74b]. -/
@[category textbook, AMS 11]
theorem Nat.Prime.h_eq_add_one {n : ℕ} (hn : 2 < n) : h n = n + 1 ↔ (n + 1).Prime := by
  sorry

/-- For odd `n`, the values of `h n` form an unbounded set.
This is described as 'easy to see' in [Er74b]. -/
@[category textbook, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_770.variants.odd_h_unbounded : Unbounded (· ≤ ·) (ENat.toNat '' (h '' Odd)):= by
  sorry


/-- For every prime `p`, does the density of integers with `h n = p` exist? -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_770.parts.i : answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ p : ℕ, p.Prime → ∃ a, HasDensity {n | h n = p} a := by
  sorry

/-- Does `liminf h n = ∞`? -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_770.parts.ii : answer(sorry) ↔ liminf h atTop = ⊤ := by
  sorry

/-- Is it true that if `p` is the greatest prime such that `p - 1 ∣ n` and `p > n ^ ε`, then
`h n = p`? -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_770.parts.iii : answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ ε > 0, ∀ᶠ n in atTop,
    let p := sSup {m : ℕ | m.Prime ∧ m - 1 ∣ n}
    p > (n : ℝ) ^ (ε : ℝ) → h n = p := by
  sorry

/-- It is probably true that `h n = 3` for infinitely many `n`. -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_770.variants.three : {n | h n = 3}.Infinite := by
  sorry

end Erdos770

findings.description: The module docstring's reference list is wrong. It cites [Er49d] (Erdős, 'On the strong law of large numbers', Trans. AMS 67 (1949) 51–56) and [Ma66] (Matsuyama, 'On the strong law of large numbers', Tohoku Math. J. 18 (1966)). These two papers are about the strong law of large numbers for sums of f(n_k x) and are unrelated to h(n). They are the references of Erdős Problem 996; FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/996.lean has the identical two entries, so they were apparently copy-pasted. The actual source [Er74b] is missing from the list, although the docstrings of `Erdos770.Nat.Prime.h_eq_add_one` and `Erdos770.erdos_770.variants.odd_h_unbounded` both cite it. The mathematics is unaffected.
findings.source_evidence: erdosproblems.com/770 lists a single source, '#770 : [Er74b]'. The bib entry at erdosproblems.com/bibs/Er74b reads: 'Erdős, P., Remarks on some problems in number theory. Math. Balkanica (1974), 197-202.' The h(n) problem is on pp. 199–200 of that paper (renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1974-27.pdf): 'Denote by h(n) the smallest integer for which the numbers (2^n − 1, 3^n − 1, ..., h(n)^n − 1) are relatively prime ...'. The zbMATH review of Er49d (Trans. AMS 67, 51–56) shows it concerns lim Σ f(n_k x)/N for lacunary n_k, not h(n).
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the [Er49d] and [Ma66] entries in the module docstring with: `- [Er74b] Erdős, P., *Remarks on some problems in number theory*. Math. Balkanica 4 (1974), 197-202.`

reformulations.difference: The definition takes `sInf` over `m : ℕ∞` with `2 < m`. So `h 1 = 3`, whereas the literal prose (and a list consisting of the single number 2^1−1 = 1) would give h(1) = 2. Also `h 0 = ⊤`, because every i^0 − 1 = 0 and the gcd is 0; the source does not consider n = 0.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For n ≥ 2 we have 2^n − 1 ≥ 3, so m = 2 never satisfies the gcd condition and the `2 < m` restriction is vacuous. `m = ⊤` never qualifies, because `Finset.Icc 2 0 = ∅` has gcd 0. The condition is upward closed. Erdős's Lemma (no prime divides all k^n − 1 for 2 ≤ k ≤ n+1) gives h(n) ≤ n+1. So for every n ≥ 2 the Lean `h n` is the source's h(n). Only n ∈ {0, 1} differ, and no statement in the file is sensitive to that: densities, `liminf`, `∀ᶠ`, `Set.Infinite` and unboundedness ignore finitely many values, and `h_eq_add_one` assumes `2 < n`. This is the same situation as the Erdős 295 helper off-by-one. The Lean convention also matches OEIS A263647 (which lists n = 1) and the convention used by the proof claim on the site. In Lean I proved `h 0 = ⊤`, `h 1 = 3`, `h 4 = 5`, `h 11 = 5`, and checked a computable mirror for n ≤ 200; the general agreement for n ≥ 2 is argued on paper.

reformulations.difference: The source says 'if p is the greatest prime such that p−1 ∣ n and p > n^ε then h(n) = p' and leaves the quantifiers implicit. The Lean makes them explicit as `∀ ε > 0, ∀ᶠ n in atTop` (for every ε, for all sufficiently large n). It also moves `p > n^ε` from the definition of p into a hypothesis about the greatest prime with p−1 ∣ n.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: (1) Let P = max{p prime : p−1 ∣ n}. The greatest prime p with (p−1 ∣ n and p > n^ε) exists iff P > n^ε, and then it equals P. So the Lean's hypothesis-form is equivalent. (2) The 'for all n' reading is trivially false: n = 11 gives P = 2 > 11^ε for ε < 0.289 while h(11) = 5, and n = 4044 gives P = 13, h = 17. The 'for some ε' reading is trivially true: with ε = 1, P > n forces P = n+1 prime, and h(n) = n+1. So 'for every ε > 0 and n ≥ n₀(ε)' is the only non-degenerate reading. It is also monotone in ε, so including large ε costs nothing. Erdős's own wording is 'It is possible that if A(n) is large (say > n^ε) then A(n) = h(n)'. The erdosproblems forum reads it the same way: 'this has to be interpreted for any ε>0' and 'we have to think as n to be sufficiently large for every ε'.

review.notes:
The only finding is a minor one; every declaration states what the source poses.

- `h`: collective gcd over 2..m with m > 2, matching Erdős's "relatively prime" (his Lemma's proof uses exactly this collective meaning).
- `Nat.Prime.h_eq_add_one`: "h(n)=n+1 iff n+1 prime", categorised as textbook.
  - The `2 < n` hypothesis drops n = 1, which it must because Lean has h 1 = 3. It also drops n = 2 unnecessarily, but that case is true, so this is a harmless weakening, not a defect.
  - Checked computationally for 3 ≤ n ≤ 200.
- `odd_h_unbounded`: `Unbounded (· ≤ ·)` unfolds to ∀ M, ∃ odd n, M < (h n).toNat. For odd n ≥ 1, `h n` is finite.
- `parts.i`: `HasDensity` is the standard natural density on ℕ, with a real-valued limit.
- `parts.ii`: `liminf h atTop = ⊤ ↔ h n → ∞`, which I proved in Lean.
  - The polarity matches erdosproblems' question "Does liminf h(n) = ∞?".
  - Erdős's own remark, "I can not prove that h(n) does not tend to infinity", and his belief that h(n) = 3 infinitely often point to the answer being no. With `answer(sorry)` this does not matter.
- `parts.iii`: see reformulations.
- `variants.three`: `{n | h n = 3}.Infinite` is exactly A263647 being infinite (the Ailon–Rudnick special case), which is open.

Status is current. erdosproblems.com shows OPEN (page last edited 24 Sep 2025), and the teorth database says open. The one proof claim, from July 2026, is explicitly partial: it proves h(n) = P(n) when P(n) > 2√n, which settles part (iii) only for ε > 1/2, and says "the density, liminf, and general ε>0 questions remain unresolved". The `research open` tags on parts i–iii and `variants.three` are therefore correct, and the textbook tags fit the source's "easy to see".

I did not read the local git history or the diffs of earlier commits to this file, to keep the review independent.
